extracted.intended_audience: mathematics researchers and academics (faculty, postdocs, graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for mathematicians on writing referee reports, giving talks, preparing a curriculum vitae, and writing grant proposals; focuses on what constitutes good practice and evaluative criteria in these academic tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of referee report
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the report in a timely manner—if possible within the time frame suggested by the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refereeing is an important professional duty; meet the editor's suggested deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear statement of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell it as you see it. Enunciate your opinion clearly and succinctly, defend it, and then summarize your findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like a letter of recommendation: state verdict, give reasons, and conclude with a summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiated defense of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Defend your opinion in detail. Read enough of the paper to comment knowledgeably and be confident about the paper's correctness and importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not check every detail or read every reference, but you must be able to justify your judgment about correctness and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Littlewood's three precepts for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: When you evaluate a paper you should address Littlewood’s three precepts: (1) Is it new? (2) Is it correct? (3) Is it surprising?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speak to the paper's contribution to knowledge and to the literature when applying these three questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess contribution to literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak to its contribution to our knowledge, and to the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the paper advances or fits into existing work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide constructive criticisms of the writing, or of the paper’s organization. Point out mathematical errors or unclear reasoning, but do not be captious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may enumerate spelling/grammar errors if you wish, but focus on substantive improvements rather than petty fault-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the paper in context: How does it compare to other recent papers in the field? Where does it fit? Does it represent progress?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether, if you were not the referee, the paper would be one you'd want to read; compare to recent literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor to journal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor your report to the journal to which the paper was submitted and base your assessment on that journal’s value system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different journals have different expectations (e.g., Annals vs more modest journals); speak to people in language they understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a specific recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important attribute of a referee’s report is that it makes a specific recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everything else is for the record; length is typically one to five pages (rarely more), but the key is a clear recommendation (accept/revise/reject/etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your subject cold (for talks)
rubrics_metrics.description: You must know your subject cold: background, biases, reasons for questions, good and bad attacks, and the current state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the material deeply means you can teach it, not merely communicate it to another similar expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-restraint in talks
rubrics_metrics.description: A good mathematics lecture is an exercise in self-restraint: do not try to say everything; showcase a nugget of knowledge and shore it up with crisp comments and incisive examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid impressing with erudition; focus on a central idea and develop it clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered accessibility of talk
rubrics_metrics.description: If your talk is 50 minutes, the first 20 minutes should be accessible to a graduate student who has passed quals; the next 20 to a mathematically literate non-specialist; the last 10 for experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to level the playing field; ramp up sophistication in stages so different audience members take something away.

rubrics_metrics.name: End with a strong conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to finish with a bang; prepare introductory and concluding sentences in advance and end by saying something meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weak closings like 'I guess that's all'; consider concluding with substantive mathematical sentences or polite remarks of thanks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor talk to talk type and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize types of talks (colloquium, seminar, job talk) and adapt content and depth accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seminars are for specialists, colloquia for broader audiences, job talks are performative—know your audience and adjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus talk on one main point
rubrics_metrics.description: Showcase one theorem, or perhaps a single cluster of theorems; avoid giving a talk on five truly different theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat the main point like a theme with variations so the audience retains the central message; for surveys, narrow the scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have an attractive, concise title
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a title that conveys the spirit and invites a broad audience rather than a long technical phrase that deters attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a succinct, compelling title (e.g., 'A new attack on a class of nonelliptic equations') over an unwieldy technical title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove something or work a detailed example
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a proof of a special case or a worked example to illustrate the main ideas and then sketch the full proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing inner workings or an example helps draw in students and non-experts and demonstrates substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure audience takes something away
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure your talk so that audience members can state what the talk was about or what the main theorem was.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep clear goals in mind while composing the talk to produce a focused presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific, avoid vague fluff
rubrics_metrics.description: Heed specificity both in writing and speaking; avoid appearing evasive or that you are dodging the main point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples and explicit statements help avoid impressions of sloppiness or fakery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow speculation and informality in talks
rubrics_metrics.description: In talks you may discuss things tried and failed and speculate about future directions; you may downplay technical points when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lie or mislead; but you can omit technical details and be informally candid about open directions to engage the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare multiple entry and exit points
rubrics_metrics.description: Design talks with multiple entry points (for drifting listeners to re-enter) and multiple exit points (to end gracefully if needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate interruptions and variable time usage; avoid a hasty 'I'm out of time' finish and do not run overtime (more than a couple minutes is rude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare thoroughly: have notes, practice, and use a preparation technique that works for you (writing out the talk, mental rehearsal, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be a slave to notes during the talk; aim to think through the ideas with the audience and engage them directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give proper credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful in your talk to give credit where it is due; do not obscure or minimize others' contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute others' results fully rather than abbreviating names only when your own name is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackboard technique
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a blackboard, write in straight horizontal lines, write large and neatly, avoid cluttering a board, and let the audience copy before erasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan board usage in advance, isolate material for later reference, and avoid blocking the board or creating a chaotic display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use slides wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Each slide should contain one thought or idea, about six to eight lines, wide margins, bottom 2 inches left blank; abbreviate rather than full sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for roughly one slide per two to three minutes; consider SliTEX for big fonts; handwritten slides can be effective too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading slides
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put too much material per slide or use too many slides; avoid printing entire long TEX documents onto transparencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too much text makes slides unreadable and overwhelms the audience; curate content per slide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management in talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit material into the allotted time; do not run overtime—it's rude and impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the talk knowing the invitation parameters and rehearse to ensure timing; running over can harm professional reputation (example: candidate who pushed clock back).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with body and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use body movement and voice to engage the audience; look at individuals, change focus and depth as the talk develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pace around, step forward/back, and avoid merely reciting to a single friend in the front row.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vita layout and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Your Curriculum Vitae should be a tableau, not paragraph form: name in bold at top, followed quickly by birth date, education, contact info, employment record, key honors, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present information so the reader can quickly pick out what they need; sample Vita shows expected fields and formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate publication list appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: List publications in a separate section; distinguish published vs unpublished, refereed vs nonrefereed, and list books separately; use approximate chronological order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some list reverse chronological; include class notes or software if relevant to your field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant listing details in Vita
rubrics_metrics.description: When listing grants, include funding agency, title and number of the grant, the amount, and the year(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, verifiable details as institutions often verify grants and funded projects offices keep records.

rubrics_metrics.name: List invited talks, students, teaching, and skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Include invited/major talks, graduate students directed, teaching experience (courses taught, curricula developed), computing/software accomplishments, and language skills if relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior academics may highlight created courses/textbooks; early-career candidates should show range and depth of teaching and technical skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include service and editorial activities
rubrics_metrics.description: A Vita may include editorial activities, service to professional societies, and other miscellaneous professional contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a catch-all section for additional relevant professional activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor the Vita to circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Customize the Vita content to your career stage: omit exhaustive lists if senior and highlight major contributions; early-career scholars should detail teaching and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be complete about expected activities for your stage (e.g., graduate student supervision is not expected of beginners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and honesty in the Vita
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not exaggerate or misstate items on your Vita; be extra careful as departments check facts and may require bona fide reprints or documented letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False or embellished claims can harm your evaluation; only list accepted publications/grants when supported by documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the grant prospectus and follow rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the prospectus for the program to learn what the program looks for and what particulars, page limits, fonts, and margins are enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant proposal writing is not free form—get the rules straight before beginning and adhere strictly to formatting and length requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate credibility in grant proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: The main issue for grants is credibility: can you do the work proposed, will you do it, and is it plausible you can make progress?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show your stature, abilities, track record, and a viable program; avoid proposing work that appears already solved or purely speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be already engaged in proposed grant work
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting agencies generally will not fund projects solely to help you learn something new; proposals should show you are already engaged and have a grip on the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a plausible case of ongoing work and partial results so funders believe you can carry the project forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the field and recent/preprint literature for grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove you are up on the relevant field—not just published literature but preprints and tentative work—since grants are refereed by cutting-edge peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will judge by their own standards; cite and situate work appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the proposal easy to read and self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: Within page limits, make the proposal as easy to read and self-contained as possible so the referee does not have to keep running to the library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your proposal engages and teaches the referee something without forcing them to look up basic background, you have an advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise and avoid verbose digressions in proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot go on at length; avoid verbose introductions or chatty conclusions and use limited pages effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on clarity, essential detail, and avoiding boredom for the reviewer.
